title: Sokółka’s Jewish Community: A World Remembered
summary: The memorial book’s central subject is the community whose religious, civic, and cultural life it records and whose destruction it mourns.
editorialContent:
![Sokółka, the town at the heart of the community](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Sok%C3%B3%C5%82ka%2C_zesp%C3%B3%C5%82_ko%C5%9Bcio%C5%82a_par._p.w._%C5%9Bw._Antoniego%2C_2_po%C5%82._XIX_01.jpg/1920px-Sok%C3%B3%C5%82ka%2C_zesp%C3%B3%C5%82_ko%C5%9Bcio%C5%82a_par._p.w._%C5%9Bw._Antoniego%2C_2_po%C5%82._XIX_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)

## A community rooted in a borderland town

The memorial book remembers Sokółka not simply as a place where Jews lived, but as a regional center of Jewish life: a town where religious study, trade, education, mutual aid and political activity gathered around familiar streets and institutions. Its chapters look back at a community that had long been woven into the town’s daily life—and at the people whose voices preserved that world after its destruction.

The book gives 1765 as a date by which Jewish residents were already established in Sokółka, but it does not claim to know when the community itself began. Its historical account says that the first Jewish presence and the founding of communal institutions are poorly documented. The book’s remembrance, then, holds two truths together: a long-standing Jewish settlement, and gaps in what can now be established about its earliest years.

Sokółka stood within a wider network of nearby towns, including [Białystok](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_f19fa262e3d446566a240656) and [Grodno](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_1e7ccce3d6546f2a8bcff778). The memorial book describes Sokółka as an economic and spiritual center, and recalls its Jewish residents as builders of local trade, industry and crafts. Yad Vashem’s account adds a different kind of evidence: before the Second World War, it estimates that about 2,800 Jews lived in Sokółka, fewer than half the town’s population, with most earning their living through commerce and crafts. Its entry also places the town in Białystok District, within the shifting political borders of the period. ([Yad Vashem, “Sokółka”](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=691))

## Prayer, study and the work of daily life

The memorial book recalls a religious landscape made up of a central synagogue and several smaller houses of prayer and study. One witness evokes the “Schulhoff,” the courtyard where children learned and played near the Great Synagogue, the old and new study houses, and the Talmud Torah. The [Sokółka synagogue](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_54393c43e6ea8a46ae33e87f) and [Sokółka cemetery](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_981054fd56848dea4761d15b) stand in the book’s account as enduring foundations of community life, though it offers little reliable detail about their earliest founders or dates.

Education joined tradition with newer cultural currents. The Sokółka Talmud Torah served children from families with different means; one memoir remembers that those who could afford it paid, while poorer children studied without charge. A woman from the Shapira family, owners of a manufacturing business, is recalled as arranging new clothes for poor pupils before Passover. Alongside traditional study, the book describes Hebrew schools and the Tarbut school, which taught Hebrew and fostered Zionist ideas. It names teachers including Hillel Levine, Nathaniel Kaplan and Nahum Kunsht.

Yad Vashem independently records a Tarbut school and a yeshiva in prewar Sokółka, as well as community welfare institutions. That account supports the broad picture of a town where religious learning, modern education and social support existed side by side, though it does not verify each detail in individual memoirs. ([Yad Vashem, “Sokółka”](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=691))

## Many institutions, many directions

The book’s picture of Sokółka is not one of a community with a single outlook. Its recollections name Zionist groups, including [Young Zion](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_8746043018e4cb3b33e2d7d3) and [Kadima](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_70e53441716a19794898cef4), as well as the [Bund](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_367e8f2dba6c93cb3d032314). The broader list of associations includes youth movements, libraries, professional organizations and a theater. Some residents imagined a future in the [Land of Israel](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_eddf4a4b356f08d00863d3f8); others took part in socialist or religious communal life. These were not merely labels. They shaped schooling, public activity and arguments about what Jewish life should become.

Mutual aid formed another part of the community’s structure. The book names *Linat ha-Tzedek*, *Gemilut Hasadim* and a soup kitchen for the poor among Sokółka’s welfare institutions. These names point to organized responses to illness, hardship and hunger; the memorial book’s accounts make clear that community life depended not only on public institutions but also on people who gave time, money and care. In neighboring communities of the region, similar associations helped residents meet needs that families could not manage alone. Such comparison supplies context, not proof of the particular routines of each Sokółka institution.

The book remembers streets as well as institutions. Białystok Street was one of the town’s two main streets, and its pages evoke shops, homes and movement through the town. What cannot be confidently reconstructed from the supplied records is the precise address of every school, charity or synagogue, or the full membership of each organization. Those unresolved details matter: they are invitations to connect family testimony with maps, photographs, directories and archival records.

## Occupation, destruction and the work of memory

The community’s institutions were not left untouched by the political upheavals of the twentieth century. The memorial book describes Soviet rule, the return of German occupation, restrictions and violence, followed by the confinement of Jews in the ghetto. Yad Vashem adds a more specific chronology: German forces returned to Sokółka on June 24, 1941; a fenced ghetto was established in autumn 1941; and on November 5, 1942, most residents were deported to the Kielbasin camp, with later deportations to Treblinka and Auschwitz. It also records the execution of Rabbi Yitzhak Halevi Schuster in Białystok in March 1942. ([Yad Vashem, “Sokółka”](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=691))

That account is an independent historical reference, not the memorial book’s own testimony. The distinction matters especially when dates, numbers or individual fates are involved. The book gathers the memories of survivors and emigrants, including people who could recall the town before the catastrophe and those who recorded the persecution. Its opening pages present the collection as a portrait of a destroyed community, assembled from memory. It is not a complete census of those who lived there: family members who emigrated, died elsewhere or appear only in archival records may be absent from its pages.

The memorial book’s achievement is therefore both intimate and limited. It restores names, teachers, streets, arguments, customs and institutions to a history that might otherwise be told only through the stages of persecution and deportation. It lets the reader see Sokółka not just as a place from which Jews were taken, but as a community whose members built schools, prayed, traded, organized, cared for one another and debated their future. The book cannot return that world, or speak for everyone who belonged to it. It does preserve a record of what survivors chose to remember—and a starting point for recovering what remains unknown.
